```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(zurand)
```

R's own generator keeps a hidden state. `set.seed()` fixes where it starts,
and every call to `runif()` or `rnorm()` moves it on, so each number depends
on everything drawn before it. zurand has no such state. In this vignette we
bootstrap the mean of a small sample, and along the way meet keys, the
samplers, key vectors and folding. Why the values are the same on every
machine, and how fast they are, is left to the articles.

## Make a key

A **key** is an immutable value made from a seed. Every random value is a
pure function of a key and the value's **position**, so the same key always
gives the same numbers:

```{r}
key <- rng_key(2026)
key
rng_uniform(key, 3)
rng_uniform(key, 3)
```

Asking for more values extends the sequence rather than changing it. The
first three of six are the three above:

```{r}
rng_uniform(key, 6)
```

Drawing uses nothing up: the key is the same afterwards, so there is no
state to pass between functions, save or restore.

## Draw from a key

The samplers are `rng_uniform()`, `rng_normal()`, `rng_integer()` and
`rng_bits()`. Each takes a key and a count, then the parameters of its
distribution. Here is the sample we will bootstrap, and one resample of
it, drawn as positions between 1 and 8:

```{r}
x <- c(2.1, 3.4, 1.9, 5.6, 4.2, 3.3, 2.8, 4.9)
i <- rng_integer(key, length(x), min = 1, max = length(x))
i
mean(x[i])
```

`rng_normal()` takes `mean` and `sd`, and `rng_uniform()` takes `min` and
`max`, in the same way.

## One key per replicate

A bootstrap needs many resamples, each from its own stream. `rng_key()`
makes a **key vector** when asked for `n` keys, and a sampler given a key
vector returns a matrix with one column per key:

```{r}
keys <- rng_key(2026, n = 200)
length(keys)
idx <- rng_integer(keys, length(x), min = 1, max = length(x))
dim(idx)
```

Each column is one resample, so the bootstrap distribution of the mean is
one line away:

```{r}
boot <- apply(idx, 2, function(i) mean(x[i]))
quantile(boot, c(0.025, 0.975))
```

A key vector can be indexed like any vector. Replicate 7 alone gives the
same resample as column 7 of the matrix, so a replicate can be rerun
without the others:

```{r}
identical(rng_integer(keys[7], length(x), min = 1, max = length(x)), idx[, 7])
```

## Name the parts with folding

Counting keys works while a computation has one part. When it has several,
derive each part's key from what the part *is*. `rng_fold()` takes a key
and some data, a name or a number, and returns a new key; the same data
always gives the same key:

```{r}
boot_key <- rng_fold(key, "bootstrap")
replicate_key <- function(b) rng_fold(boot_key, b)
rng_uniform(replicate_key(3), 2)
rng_uniform(replicate_key(3), 2)
```

Because replicate `b` gets its numbers from its own key, the bootstrap gives
the same answer whatever order the replicates run in. Here they run once in
order and once shuffled, as parallel workers might run them (`sample()`
only picks the order):

```{r}
boot_mean <- function(b) {
  i <- rng_integer(replicate_key(b), length(x), min = 1, max = length(x))
  mean(x[i])
}
in_order <- vapply(1:200, boot_mean, numeric(1))

shuffled <- numeric(200)
run_order <- sample(200)
shuffled[run_order] <- vapply(run_order, boot_mean, numeric(1))
identical(in_order, shuffled)
```

A new part of the analysis, folded under another name, cannot change these
values. The same holds for zurand's own threads: `rng_threads()` changes how
fast a large draw is made, never what it contains.

## Vectors of any length

`rng_lazy_normal()` and `rng_lazy_uniform()` return a **lazy vector**: it
holds only its key and arguments, and computes a value when it is read. A
billion values are created at once, and they are the values the ordinary
sampler gives:

```{r}
z <- rng_lazy_normal(key, 1e9)
length(z)
z[1:3]
rng_normal(key, 3)
```

## A common mistake

The samplers take a key, not a seed. Passing the seed itself is an error
that says what to do instead:

```{r, error = TRUE}
rng_normal(2026, 3)
```
